sub: Named after al-fajr, “the dawn”, the surah’s opening word
theme: Allah is always watching. Wealth and poverty are both tests, not signs of honour or disgrace, and on the Day of Judgement only what you sent ahead will count.
story: Revealed in Makkah, when the persecution of new Muslims had begun. The Makkans refused to accept that deeds would be rewarded and punished in the Hereafter.

So the surah swears by dawn and sacred nights, recalls what happened to ʿĀd, Thamūd and Pharaoh when they spread corruption, and exposes a society that treated wealth as honour, neglected orphans and devoured inheritances.
It ends on the Day when regret is useless, and with Allah’s gentle call to the soul at peace. The Prophet ﷺ named it among the surahs suitable for leading prayer.

sections.title: By the dawn and ten nights
sections.meaning: Allah swears by the dawn, by ten nights, by the even and the odd, and by the night as it passes. Isn’t that oath enough for anyone with sense?
points: By the dawn and ten nights
By the even and the odd
By the night as it moves away
Enough of an oath for one with sense?
sections.matters: These oaths point to sacred times of worship and to the steady order of night and day. A thinking person should see that the One who runs this order will also hold people to account.
sections.story: No specific incident. The ten nights are usually taken as the first ten of Dhul-Ḥijjah. The Prophet ﷺ said no days are more beloved to Allah for good deeds than these.
explained: Al-fajr: the dawn of every day, when night ends and light breaks; or one special dawn, such as that of the Day of Sacrifice. Layālin ʿashr: ten nights, most often the first ten of Dhul-Ḥijjah, or the last ten of Ramaḍān.

Ash-shafʿ wal-watr: the even and the odd. In one report, the Day of Sacrifice and the Day of ʿArafah; others say all creation in pairs, and Allah the One. The night yasr: moving on and leaving. Is that not enough for dhū ḥijr, one whose mind holds him back from wrong?
teaches: Value the dawn and the sacred ten days; Allah swears by them.
Real intelligence is a mind that stops you from wrong.
Reflect on the signs you see every day.
sections.hook: Four oaths, each starting with wa: wal-fajr, wa-layālin, wash-shafʿ, wal-layl. Dawn opens (1), night closes (4), then a question (5).

sections.title: ʿĀd, Thamūd, Pharaoh: your Lord watches
sections.meaning: Have you not seen what your Lord did to ʿĀd of Iram, with its lofty pillars, unmatched in the land; to Thamūd, who carved rock in the valley; and to Pharaoh of the stakes? They tyrannised and spread corruption, so your Lord poured a whip of punishment on them. He is always watching.
points: ʿĀd of Iram, the pillared, unmatched in the land
Thamūd, who carved rocks in the valley
A whip of punishment; your Lord lies in wait
sections.matters: History is the proof. The strongest nations were destroyed once they became tyrants, and ayah 14 is the key line of the surah: your Lord is ever watchful. Nobody slips past.
sections.story: No specific incident. Persecution of Muslims had begun in Makkah, and the Quraysh were warned with the fate of three nations far stronger than they were.
explained: ʿĀd, also called Iram, were the earlier ʿĀd, to whom Hūd was sent. Dhāt al-ʿimād: people of tall pillars, either their raised buildings or their tall, powerful bodies. No nation had been created like them in the land. Thamūd carved homes out of the rock in the valley.

Pharaoh was dhū al-awtād, owner of the stakes: either the armies that held up his rule, or the stakes he used to torture people. All of them tyrannised and filled the land with corruption, so Allah poured on them a sawṭ ʿadhāb, a lashing of punishment. Inna rabbaka la-bil-mirṣād: He watches, and nothing escapes Him.
teaches: Strength, buildings and armies cannot protect tyrants.
Oppression and corruption bring Allah’s punishment.
Allah gives time, but He is always watching.
Learn from history before becoming its warning.
sections.hook: Three nations in order: ʿĀd (6), Thamūd (9), Pharaoh (10), each with one mark: pillars, rocks, stakes. “Your Lord” appears at 6, 13 and 14.

sections.title: Wealth is a test, not honour
sections.meaning: When Allah tests man with blessings, he says “My Lord has honoured me”; when He tests him with less, he says “My Lord has humiliated me.” No! The real problem: you don’t honour the orphan, don’t urge feeding the poor, devour inheritance greedily and love wealth too much.
points: Given plenty: “My Lord has honoured me”
Given less: “My Lord has humiliated me”
No! You don’t honour orphans or urge feeding the poor
You devour inheritance and love wealth too much
sections.matters: It corrects a common mistake: judging Allah’s love by money. Wealth and poverty are both tests. What really shows a person’s standing is how he treats the weak and how tightly he clutches his wealth.
sections.story: Reportedly revealed about Umayyah ibn Khalaf. Qudāmah ibn Maẓʿūn was an orphan in his care, and he kept him from his rights. At the time, women and children were often cut out of inheritance.
explained: Ibtalāhu: Allah tests man. If He gives honour and comfort, man thinks it proves Allah favours him. If He restricts his provision, he says Allah has disgraced him. Kallā: never. Allah gives wealth to those He loves and those He doesn’t, and withholds from both. The test is gratitude in plenty and patience in hardship.

The real failing is elsewhere. You don’t honour the orphan: not just feeding him, but treating him with dignity. You don’t urge each other to feed the miskīn. You devour inheritance, grabbing everyone’s share, lawful or not. And you love wealth ḥubban jammā, with a love that never has enough.
teaches: Wealth is not proof of Allah’s love, and poverty is not proof of His anger.
Be grateful when given, patient when held back.
Honour orphans with respect, not only with money.
Encourage others to feed the poor, even if you have little.
sections.hook: Two “when He tests him” lines (15–16) end in opposite words: akraman (honoured me) and ahānan (humiliated me). Kallā answers, and the next words reuse the root: lā tukrimūna al-yatīm (17).

sections.title: The Day, and the soul at peace
sections.meaning: No! When the earth is pounded flat, your Lord comes with angels in rows, and Hell is brought near, man remembers too late and wishes he had sent good ahead. None punishes like Allah that Day. But the soul at peace hears: return to your Lord, pleased and pleasing; enter My Paradise.
points: The earth crushed flat; your Lord comes, angels in rows
Hell brought near; man remembers, too late
“If only I had sent ahead for my life”
None punishes or binds like Him
O soul at peace, return, pleased and pleasing
Enter among My servants, enter My Paradise
sections.matters: It answers the wealth-lovers of section 3: on that Day wealth is gone and only what you sent ahead remains. And it ends the surah not with fear but with a gentle welcome for the believing soul.
sections.story: Reportedly ayah 27 came while Abū Bakr sat with the Prophet ﷺ. He said nothing could be better, and was told the angel would say it to him. Other reports link it to ʿUthmān or to Khubayb ibn ʿAdī.
explained: Kallā: your wealth won’t last. The earth is pounded, dakkan dakkā, again and again until flat. Your Lord comes to judge, in a way only He knows, and the angels come rank upon rank. Hell is brought forward. Man finally remembers, but it is useless now. He cries: if only I had sent ahead for my real life.

That Day no one punishes like Allah, and no one binds like He binds. Then the other voice: yā ayyatuhā an-nafs al-muṭmaʾinnah, O soul at rest with Allah. Return to your Lord, rāḍiyah, pleased with Him, marḍiyyah, pleasing to Him. Enter among My servants. Enter My Paradise. It is said at death and on the Day of Judgement.
teaches: Send good deeds ahead now; later regret cannot help.
The real life is the one after this.
A heart at peace with Allah is the goal.
Seek the company of the righteous; Paradise is entered among them.
sections.hook: Kallā opens this section (21), as it opened ayah 17. Yawmaʾidhin (“that Day”) comes three times: twice in 23, once in 25. The page turns at ayah 23, as Hell is brought near.

groups.text: By the dawn, ten nights, the even and the odd, and the night as it passes.
Is that not an oath enough for someone with sense?
See what your Lord did to ʿĀd of Iram, the pillared, unmatched in the land.
And to Thamūd, who carved rock in the valley, and Pharaoh, man of the stakes.
They all tyrannised in the lands and spread corruption there.
So your Lord poured a whip of punishment on them. He is always watching.
Given plenty, man says Allah honoured him; given less, he says Allah humiliated him.
No! You don’t honour the orphan or urge one another to feed the poor.
You devour inheritance whole and love wealth with an endless love.
When the earth is crushed, your Lord comes with angels, and Hell is brought, man remembers, too late.
He wishes he had sent good ahead. None punishes or binds like Allah that Day.
O soul at peace, return to your Lord, pleased and pleasing to Him.
Enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise.

1.explain: Wal-fajr: by the dawn. The daybreak of every day, which shows Allah’s power, or one special dawn, such as the Day of Sacrifice or the first day of Muḥarram.

2.explain: Layālin ʿashr: ten nights. Mostly the first ten of Dhul-Ḥijjah, the best days for good deeds; others say the last ten of Ramaḍān, which hold Laylat al-Qadr.

3.explain: Ash-shafʿ wal-watr: the even and the odd. In one report, the Day of Sacrifice and the Day of ʿArafah. Others say creation in pairs and Allah the One, or even and odd prayers.

4.explain: Wal-layli idhā yasr: by the night as it moves along and departs. Some read it as the night settling in, bringing rest.

5.explain: Is there not in that a qasam, an oath enough, for dhū ḥijr? Ḥijr is the mind, because it holds a person back from what is unworthy of him.

6.explain: Alam tara: have you not seen, with your heart’s eye, what your Lord did to ʿĀd, the people of Hūd, who rejected him and were destroyed by a violent wind?

7.explain: Iram: the earlier ʿĀd. Dhāt al-ʿimād: of the pillars, either their houses raised on strong pillars or their tall stature. Some speak instead of a pillared city they built.

8.explain: No nation like them had been created in the land, in strength, power and size. They boasted, “Who is stronger than us?” (41:15).

9.explain: Thamūd jābū aṣ-ṣakhr: they cut through the rock in the valley, carving homes out of the mountains with their strength.

10.explain: Pharaoh dhū al-awtād, of the stakes: either his armies, which held his rule firm like pegs, or the stakes he tied or nailed people to for torture.

11.explain: Alladhīna ṭaghaw: all three nations tyrannised in the lands, harming Allah’s servants in their faith and their lives.

12.explain: They multiplied fasād: disbelief and every kind of sin, killing, fighting the messengers and blocking people from Allah’s way.

13.explain: Sawṭ ʿadhāb: a whip of punishment. A whip lands again and again, so they suffered punishment of many kinds, poured on them.

14.explain: La-bil-mirṣād: at the lookout, like one waiting on a narrow pass. Allah watches every deed; He gives the disobedient time, then seizes them.

15.explain: Tested with honour and comfort, man says: my Lord has honoured me, as if blessings proved Allah’s love for him.
15.why: Reportedly revealed about Umayyah ibn Khalaf, a disbeliever of Makkah.

16.explain: Tested with limited provision, he says: my Lord has humiliated me. Both conditions are tests, of gratitude and of patience.

17.explain: Kallā: not so! Honour is not measured by wealth. Bal lā tukrimūna al-yatīm: you don’t give the orphan his rights or treat him with dignity.
17.why: Reportedly about Qudāmah ibn Maẓʿūn, an orphan raised by Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who kept him from his rights.

18.explain: Lā taḥāḍḍūna: you don’t urge one another to feed the miskīn. Even those with little can encourage others to give.

19.explain: At-turāth: inheritance. Aklan lammā: devouring it all together, your share and others’, lawful or not. Women and children were often denied their shares.

20.explain: Ḥubban jammā: an overflowing love of wealth. Some love of money is natural; what is blamed is excessive love that is never satisfied.

21.explain: Kallā: stop! Dakkan dakkā: the earth is pounded again and again until every mountain and building is levelled.

22.explain: Your Lord comes to judge between His creation, in a way only He knows, and the angels come ṣaffan ṣaffā, rank after rank.

23.explain: Hell is brought forward; the Prophet ﷺ said it will have 70,000 reins, each pulled by 70,000 angels. Man remembers his deeds, but what use is remembering now?

24.explain: Yā laytanī qaddamtu li-ḥayātī: if only I had sent good ahead for my life, the lasting life. Even the obedient will wish they had done more.

25.explain: That Day no one punishes like Allah punishes those who ignored that Day.

26.explain: And no one binds like He binds, with chains and fetters. This is the recompense of the wrongdoers.

27.explain: An-nafs al-muṭmaʾinnah: the soul at rest, calm through remembering Allah, certain of Him and content with His decree.
27.why: Reportedly revealed while Abū Bakr sat with the Prophet ﷺ, who told him this would be said to him. Other reports link it to ʿUthmān giving the well of Rūmah, or to Khubayb ibn ʿAdī.

28.explain: Irjiʿī: return to your Lord, rāḍiyah, pleased with Him and His reward, marḍiyyah, with Him pleased with you. Said at death, and again on the Day of Judgement.

29.explain: Enter among My servants: first join the righteous, whose company is such a blessing that prophets prayed for it.

30.explain: And enter My Paradise. Allah calls it “My Paradise”, an honour showing it is the home of His pleasure.
